current.lab_name: Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University (Guangzhou, China)
current.role: Last author of a study of scleral autophagy in form-deprivation myopia.
current.sub: Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University · Aier Eye Hospital Group
story: Xiaoxiao Zhang was last author of the Atlas study WEN2026 in the FASEB Journal. It used human scleral cells and guinea pigs with experimental myopia. Too much autophagy in the sclera (the white of the eye) seemed to link low-oxygen stress to remodelling of the tissue. Rapamycin under the conjunctiva made myopia worse, 3-MA eased it, and atropine slowed it. AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling was measured, but the paper does not show it is the route that causes the effect. PubMed lists Zhang at Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University, Guangzhou.

highlights.WEN2026: Last author: senior author of the guinea pig and cell study on scleral autophagy in myopia.

pubmed_affiliation: Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China.

studies.title: Role of Autophagy in Scleral Remodeling During Form-Deprivation Myopia
studies.finding: Excess scleral autophagy links hypoxic stress to extracellular matrix remodelling in experimental myopia. In form-deprived guinea pigs, subconjunctival rapamycin made myopia worse and 3-MA alleviated it, while atropine slowed myopia and suppressed autophagy-related changes. AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling was measured, but the paper does not establish it as the mediating route.

current.role: First author of a 2026 fission yeast study of resistance to TORC1 inhibitors.
current.sub: School of Pharmacy · Chengdu University · Chengdu, China
story: Lufeng Dan is first author of a 2026 paper in Microbiology Spectrum. In fission yeast, resistance to rapamycin plus caffeine came and went from one generation to the next. The team found that this was not an epigenetic switch. Instead, loss-of-function mutations in the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and reverted to the normal sequence when resistance was lost. Gaf1 encodes a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. PubMed lists him at the School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University.

highlights.DAN2026: First author of the yeast study tracing reversible TORC1 inhibitor resistance to gaf1 mutations.

pubmed_affiliation: Antibiotics Innovation and Resistance Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University, Chengdu, China.

studies.title: Recurrent reversible mutations at gaf1 driving metastable TORC1 inhibitor resistance in fission yeast.
studies.finding: Metastable resistance to TORC1 inhibitors (rapamycin plus caffeine) in fission yeast is driven by recurrent, spontaneously reversible loss-of-function mutations in gaf1, a GATA transcription factor and negative growth regulator downstream of TORC1 - a genetic (not epigenetic) toggle that can silently contaminate lab yeast stocks.

story: Christine M Chresta was first author of a 2009 paper in Cancer Research. PubMed lists the author at AstraZeneca in Cheshire, UK.

The paper describes AZD8055, a drug that blocks the mTOR kinase directly and so inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2, including outputs that rapamycin leaves untouched. It was tested in cancer cells and in mouse tumour models, where it slowed growth. Chresta is also listed on a 2009 Dundee paper in the Atlas, but PubMed gives no affiliation for that record, so it is not covered here.

story: Sabina Cosulich is a middle author of a 2016 paper in Nature. PubMed lists her at AstraZeneca in Alderley Park, Macclesfield, UK, while the first authors were at Memorial Sloan Kettering and UCSF.

The study found how cancer cells become resistant to mTOR kinase inhibitors, through mutations that raise mTOR's own activity. It then built RapaLink-1, a bivalent third-generation inhibitor that still works against those mutants in cells and mice. A 2009 AZD8055 paper in the Atlas lists the same name, but its PubMed record gives no affiliation, so it is not covered here.

highlights.ROD2016: Middle author of the study that developed RapaLink-1 to overcome mTOR resistance mutations.

story: Ellen Kraig is first author of an Atlas study (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was short and small. PubMed lists Kraig at the Barshop Institute and the Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio. Her name also appears on a 2012 mouse paper (MAJ2012), but PubMed gives no affiliation for her there, so it was not counted.

highlights.KRA2018: First author: reported the pilot trial of rapamycin safety, immune markers, physical performance and cognition in older adults.

pubmed_affiliation: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, The University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, USA; Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, The University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, USA.

studies.title: A randomized control trial to establish the feasibility and safety of rapamycin treatment in an older human cohort: Immunological, physical performance, and cognitive effects.
studies.finding: A safety-first pilot RCT (n=25, ages 70-95) asking the basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe in healthy older people? Over 8+ weeks it was well tolerated with only minor red-blood-cell changes and - importantly - NO rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance in this short window. Groundwork for larger aging trials like PEARL.

story: Elizabeth Fernandez is a middle author of two studies of oral rapamycin in the common marmoset, a small monkey. The 2014 study set out dosing and blood levels and saw reduced mTORC1 signalling in treated animals. The 2015 study found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment.

studies.title: Metabolic consequences of long-term rapamycin exposure on common marmoset monkeys (Callithrix jacchus).
studies.finding:
Long-term oral encapsulated rapamycin in marmosets had only minor metabolic consequences. Body weight was unchanged overall and fat mass fell only slightly over the first few months. Daily activity counts, blood lipids and glucose metabolism, including oral glucose tolerance, did not change significantly, and adipose tissue showed no difference in metabolic-marker gene expression. In liver, G6Pase activity was suppressed while PCK and GPI activity increased.
Boundary: marmoset, oral rapamycin, metabolic endpoints only; the abstract gives neither the dose nor group sizes, and no lifespan result is reported.

studies.title: Lifespan benefits for the combination of rapamycin plus acarbose and for captopril in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.finding: NIA Interventions Testing Program C2017 cohort. In MALE mice, rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months produced a longer lifespan than either of the two prior ITP cohorts treated with rapamycin alone, suggesting the combination is more potent than its components used separately. In FEMALES the combination was neither better nor worse than rapamycin alone, which the authors relate to the limited survival benefit acarbose alone had shown in earlier female cohorts. Captopril gave a small but significant lifespan increase in females (4-5%). current.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2016)
story: Matthew Lelegren was first author of a 2016 paper on marmosets treated with rapamycin (LEL2016), from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of a core proteasome subunit, although proteasome activity did not change. Helper proteins in mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. The effects depended on the tissue.

highlights.LEL2016: First author; PubMed lists the author at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute.

pubmed_affiliation: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, San Antonio, TX, USA.

studies.title: Pharmaceutical inhibition of mTOR in the common marmoset: effect of rapamycin on regulators of proteostasis in a non-human primate.
studies.finding:
In liver and skeletal muscle from rapamycin-treated marmosets (the earlier pilot cohort), rapamycin was associated with higher expression of PSMB5, a core 20S proteasome subunit, in both tissues but not of PSMB8; proteasome activity itself did not change. Mitochondria-targeted chaperones rose in skeletal muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue but not liver. The authors conclude that only some components of the proteostasis network were upregulated, and in a tissue-specific way.
Boundary: tissue samples from a small pilot cohort; the changes are expression-level associations and are not shown to cause any health or lifespan effect.

story: Glyn Nelson is a co-author on two cell-biology papers in the Atlas, both from Newcastle University. PubMed lists him at the Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences in 2017 and the Biosciences Institute in 2024. He is second author on the 2017 paper and a middle author on the 2024 one.

The 2017 paper found that mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent human fibroblasts and no longer responds to nutrient removal. The 2024 paper found that routine clearing of damaged mitochondria shuts down in senescent and aged cells. Both were done in cultured human cells.

studies.title: Persistent mTORC1 signaling in cell senescence results from defects in amino acid and growth factor sensing
studies.finding: Explains why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells. In human fibroblasts rendered senescent three different ways, mTORC1 is constitutively active and no longer responds to serum or amino acid withdrawal. The defect is upstream, not in mTORC1 itself: it is driven in part by depolarisation of the senescent plasma membrane, which leads to primary cilia defects and a failure to shut off growth-factor signalling, while increased autophagy and high intracellular amino acid levels may act to support the nutrient arm. Correcting these inputs restored sensitivity of the pathway and killed the cells, which frames persistent mTORC1 signalling as a survival dependency of senescent cells rather tha

studies.title: Suppressed basal mitophagy drives cellular aging phenotypes that can be reversed by a p62-targeting small molecule
studies.finding: Healthy primary human cells run a high level of basal mitophagy, started by mitochondrial superoxide and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the selective receptor. That housekeeping shuts down on entry into senescence and in naturally aged cells. Blocking mitophagy in young proliferating cells was by itself enough to trigger the senescence program, and reactivation of mitophagy was necessary for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin and of NAD precursors, which places part of rapamycin's action on cellular ageing downstream of mitochondrial quality control rather than beside it. A p62-targeting small molecule restored mitophagy and rescued markers of cellular ageing.

current.sub: Biosciences Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle University, UK
story: George Kelly is first author of an Atlas study (KEL2024) in primary human cells. Healthy cells ran a steady level of mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria, through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor. This shut down as cells became senescent or old. Blocking mitophagy in young cells triggered senescence, and restarting it was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to work against senescence. PubMed lists Kelly at the Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University.

highlights.KEL2024: First author: reported that suppressed basal mitophagy drives senescence in human cells and that a p62-targeting small molecule can reverse it.

story: This biochemical study showed that raptor, a partner protein of mTOR, binds mTOR targets such as p70 S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 through short sequences called TOS motifs. That makes raptor the part of mTORC1 that presents substrates to the kinase. Nojima is the first of ten authors, and PubMed lists the Biosignal Research Center at Kobe University.

story: Two Atlas studies list Sujuti Hidayat as a middle author. Both are cell-biology papers on raptor, the protein that sits beside mTOR. One showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6K1, and that silencing it in worms mimics loss of TOR. The other showed that raptor grabs these two substrates through a short TOS motif.

PubMed lists no affiliation for him in these records. A 2003 paper on which he is first author shares four co-authors with both studies and places him at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

story: This 2017 study used a mouse model in which mTOR drives fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer. The team found that mTORC2 promotes de novo synthesis of fats and lipids, and that blocking fatty acid or sphingolipid synthesis prevented tumours. Higher lipid synthesis also tracked with mTORC2 activity in liver cancer patients.
Paul Jenoe is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists the affiliation shown here. Other Atlas records under this name show no affiliation in PubMed, so they are not included.

story: The team deleted rictor, a core part of mTORC2, only in mouse liver. The liver then lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and kept making glucose while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not tell the animal had eaten. The mice developed high blood sugar and insulin and low blood lipids.
Asami Hagiwara is first author. PubMed lists her at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.

highlights.HAG2012: First author of the liver-specific rictor knockout study.

pubmed_affiliation: Biozentrum, University of Basel, CH-4056 Basel, Switzerland.

studies.title: Hepatic mTORC2 activates glycolysis and lipogenesis through Akt, glucokinase, and SREBP1c
studies.finding:
The authors deleted rictor, an essential mTORC2 component, only in mouse liver. In fed knockout mice the liver lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and had lower glucokinase and SREBP1c activity, so it kept making glucose (gluconeogenesis) while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice became hyperglycaemic and hyperinsulinaemic with low blood lipids. In mTORC2-deficient hepatocytes, constitutively active Akt2 restored both glucose flux and lipogenesis, while extra glucokinase restored glucose flux but not lipogenesis, placing Akt as the main route from hepatic mTORC2 to these outputs.
Boundary: Mouse liver with lifelong genetic loss of mTORC
